title: Band directors' question: how will my kid earn a living?
summary: The most common question from parents and band directors is about earning a living in music; Herman says if music is the kid's overriding desire they'll do it anyway.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Now, you're always involved yourself in these visits to campuses, somewhere or another beyond -- maybe talking to the kids. You have sessions that are seminars just for the band directors, don't you?
-- most important facet, if any, I think, to be able to answer some questions about what goes on out here in this part of the world.
Well, what do you feel seems to be the most pressing things they're concerned with? That they want to communicate to their students? Does that come out at all?

I think the number one thing that I'm asked, and there is no real answer to it, it stems from the parents and finally gets to the band director, and to everybody else. But that is: When the kid finally makes up his mind when he gets out of high school he's going to Berklee, Berkeley, or he's going to North Texas or he's going to wherever he is, and he's going to major
and live music, and then his parents will most times say, 'How are you going to earn a living?'

And it starts there and works down. And so the band directors get this asked of them every other day, and why should I buy him a new saxophone or a new flute? We don't want him to be a musician. We want them to play, that's fine, but we don't want him to be a musician.

And there are no answers to these things, except that I have a stock routine I do to all the kids. I tell them -- and if their parents ask me, I give them the same answer, and that is simply if music has gotten to a point with you where you'd rather eat, sleep and drink that than anything else, and if your desire is so heavy, you're going to do it, anyway.
And when all you tell your kid or all you're going to do to change he or she, it's not going to make it, it's going to be their own decision, in the final analysis.
But I never encourage the kid to say -- it's great, or you'll make it -- (inaudible), no way.
